text: Photosensitization: red, swollen skin that blisters and cracks, with skin patches sloughing off. Causes: drug hypersensitivity (e.g. to sulfa drugs), fungus on Brachiaria grass, or liver damage (e.g. from Fasciola) that leaves the animal unable to clear toxins normally. Treatment: shade, Dexamethasone at the early stage, or Amoxicillin LA if there's significant crusting. Discoloration: hair/skin color changes usually track with poor body condition and a rough coat, commonly from vitamin A, zinc, or copper deficiency (or simply from an old insect bite or healed injury growing back different-colored hair); one or two vitamin injections rarely fix it, since minerals and vitamins work together and correcting a deficiency needs several weeks of a well-balanced daily diet — distributing concentrate feed for 3–4 weeks is the best approach. Wounds: all wounds bleed, hurt, and risk infection or maggot invasion (if maggots are present, spray insecticide like Raid into the wound, wait a few minutes, then remove them with a clipper before treating as a normal wound). Treatment: thorough washing with plenty of water and gentle brushing is about 90% of proper wound care; cut away surrounding hair; apply iodine if the wound is clean, or a Tetracycline + Gentian Violet spray otherwise; inject a long-acting antibiotic (Amoxicillin LA, Oxytetracycline LA) for deep wounds. Warts: caused by papillomavirus, picked up from contaminated branches while grazing in bush and entering through small skin breaks; cattle generally aren't otherwise sick, there's no treatment, and warts typically shrink and fall off within 3–6 months on their own.
